title: The global munitions crisis requires Foreign Military Sales reform
gist: The US foreign military sales bureaucracy (AECA/FMS process) is too slow to keep pace with a global munitions crisis exposed by the 2026 Iran-Gulf missile exchanges; the author argues Trump's 2025 executive orders give the administration tools to speed emergency replenishment, co-production, and reclassification to Direct Commercial Sales without new legislation.

insights.claim: Global conflict demand for weapons is expanding faster than US industry's capacity to manufacture munitions, and even where production keeps pace, outdated defense sales processes are the binding constraint on getting equipment to allies.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Defense contractors and munitions suppliers face a demand backdrop constrained less by factory capacity than by sales-process throughput; process reform, not just production capex, is the near-term lever.
insights.quote: Global conflict is expanding faster than the United States’ capacity to manufacture weapons.

insights.claim: During 2026's Operation Epic Fury (Iranian missile and drone barrages on US Gulf partners in response to US/Israeli strikes on Iran), the extreme munitions burn rate fully exposed how vulnerable US and allied air-defense stockpiles are to sustained high-intensity exchanges.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Interceptor and air-defense munitions demand (e.g., Patriot-class systems) should be modeled against sustained high-burn-rate regional conflict scenarios, not peacetime replenishment assumptions.
insights.quote: Consumption of advanced munitions during Operation Epic Fury fully exposed the vulnerability in such an extreme burn rate.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "The arms delivery crisis became evident"

insights.claim: New foreign orders for US defense articles do not subtract from US military stocks because defense articles are made-to-order for both domestic and foreign buyers, undercutting the argument that faster arms sales to allies would come at the expense of US readiness.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Removes a common political objection to accelerating FMS approvals, strengthening the case that reform is primarily a bureaucratic-speed problem, which is investable via defense-sales-process beneficiaries and contractors with expanding foreign order books.
insights.quote: Defense articles are only made-to-order, regardless of whether they are for domestic or foreign sales. New orders from partner countries do not take away from US stocks and only help the efficacy of the domestic defense industrial base.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "A full solution to replenishing"

insights.claim: The threat of conflict in the Indo-Pacific means the current Gulf-driven munitions strain is not the worst-case scenario the US defense industrial base will have to face.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Munitions and interceptor demand could see a second, larger surge if Indo-Pacific tensions escalate, layering on top of already-strained Gulf and Ukraine replenishment needs.
insights.quote: the threat of conflict in the Indo-Pacific serves as a stark reminder that the worst has yet to occur.

insights.claim: The Arms Export Control Act-governed FMS process involves State Department approval, DSCA administration, interagency coordination, congressional notification, and contracting steps that together can take years to convert a partner country's formal request into a signed contract, before production and delivery even begin.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Total lead time from ally request to delivered equipment can span many years, meaning current-year FMS backlogs are a leading indicator of defense contractor order books several years out.
insights.quote: it takes years for a foreign government’s formal request to result in a contract—on top of the several years it can take for production and delivery of equipment.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "This process is intended to ensure"

insights.claim: The administration can invoke the AECA's emergency authority provision—used previously in 1979, 1984, 1990, and 2019 in response to Iranian threats—to waive the congressional review period and rapidly replenish Gulf air defense stocks.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: A precedent-backed emergency waiver mechanism is available now for Gulf air-defense resupply, meaning near-term FMS acceleration to Gulf states does not require any legislative change — watch for its invocation as a leading signal of expedited defense sales.

insights.claim: Three concrete near-term reforms are available under existing law: continued use of AECA emergency authority for Gulf air defense, expanded co-production of defense equipment with Gulf partners as a long-term supply fix, and reclassification of items from FMS to the faster Direct Commercial Sales track where the original 'sensitive' criteria no longer apply.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Co-production deals and FMS-to-DCS reclassifications are actionable catalysts to watch for in Gulf defense contracts — they would signal faster contractor revenue recognition and reduced US-government bottleneck risk.

insights.claim: President Trump's 2025 executive orders 'Reforming Foreign Defense Sales' and 'Establishing an America First Arms Transfer Strategy' already set in motion a streamlined, consolidated approval process meant to prioritize key partner countries and articles for expedited handling.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: These executive orders are the policy lever the administration can lean on right now to cut FMS timelines without needing Congress — a factor for forecasting how quickly pending Gulf and Ukraine arms deals convert to contracts.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "The executive branch can move"

insights.claim: Applying the Defense Technology Security Administration's 'release in principle' determination to all recurring Gulf air defense replenishment needs would give partners conceptual pre-approval, significantly expediting the FMS process and providing clarity on which sales are viable.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: A DTSA blanket pre-approval mechanism for recurring Gulf air-defense sales would materially shorten deal cycle times for interceptor and air-defense suppliers selling into the region.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "Additionally, the administration could designate"

insights.claim: Gulf partner countries achieved interception rates above 90 percent against thousands of Iranian drones and missiles, a success attributed largely to US-built Integrated Air and Missile Defense (IAMD) architecture linking US, Israeli, and Gulf sensors and interceptors.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: This interception track record is the strongest current argument for Gulf states to keep buying US-integrated air defense systems rather than diversifying suppliers, supporting continued demand for US interceptor and radar/sensor makers.
insights.quote: The success Gulf countries had in intercepting thousands of Iranian drones and missiles—with over 90 percent interception rates across the Gulf—was in large part due to US IAMD efforts and US equipment and training.

insights.claim: US Central Command has been deliberately shifting from a 'security guarantor' role to a 'security integrator' role in the Gulf, building a regional Integrated Air and Missile Defense network years before the 2026 Iran war began.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: This is a structural, multi-year US strategic pivot in the Gulf (not a one-off reaction to the Iran war), implying durable demand for integrated air-defense architecture and interoperable equipment across the region.

insights.claim: As talk grows of US troop withdrawal or disengagement from the Middle East, accelerating arms sales is framed as a tool for the US to retain access and influence with Gulf partners even as its physical military footprint shrinks.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Arms sales volume could substitute for troop presence as the primary lever of US Gulf influence — a bullish signal for defense exporters even under a broader US regional drawdown narrative.
insights.quote: As talk grows of US disengagement or troop withdrawals from the Middle East, and elsewhere, ramping up arms sales can ensure the US sustains access and influence.

insights.claim: A 2024 Defense Security Cooperation Agency-commissioned study found that the State and Defense Departments need to further identify, clarify, and codify their respective FMS responsibilities, reflecting persistent interagency tension between the two agencies that slows reform.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Interagency turf friction between State and Defense is an underappreciated structural drag on FMS speed that executive orders alone may not fully resolve, a risk factor for how quickly announced reforms actually translate into faster contracts.
insights.locator: Addressing concerns about FMS reforms section
